events.title: VALERIUS MAKES THE LOOSE PHALANX A REPEATED FIELD DRILL
events.body: Valerius begins the week by making the loose-phalanx arrangement a repeated field drill rather than a formation used only when the column is stopped. The men practice keeping deliberate intervals while the outermost files face away from the interior and the men inside remain able to move toward another section. The exercise is conducted over uneven ground so that the formation is tested where a perfectly ordered parade arrangement would be least useful. Valerius repeatedly shifts attention from the forward edge to the flanks and rear, requiring the men to preserve awareness in more than one direction at once. The scribes record the practice as an established expedition doctrine, while the military establishment itself remains unchanged.

events.title: THE SURVEY PARTY FOLLOWS THE ENGINEERED ROAD TO A BROKEN CROSSING
events.body: The expedition follows the engineered road farther than the previously inspected section and reaches a crossing whose prepared approach has been damaged by erosion and accumulated debris. The roadbed remains visible on both sides, but the break prevents the party from claiming that the original route continues intact beyond the crossing. The scribes measure the visible construction and mark the interruption without assigning a builder, date, or final destination to the work. The formation allows the survey party to work at the crossing while the outer files continue watching the surrounding approaches. The damaged crossing becomes another concrete piece of evidence in the route investigation rather than proof of the purpose for which the road was built.

events.title: AN OLD LINE OF MARKERS APPEARS BESIDE A SECONDARY APPROACH
events.body: A secondary approach draws the attention of the outer watch when a line of weathered stones appears beside the track where the vegetation has thinned. The stones are too indistinct to identify as Roman milestones, boundary markers, or any other specific official work, and no inscription survives that would settle their purpose. Valerius orders the feature recorded exactly as observed rather than allowing the men to assign it a convenient explanation. The formation permits a small group to examine the markers while the remainder of the perimeter stays attentive to the surrounding ground. The discovery gives the route inquiry another lead, but it does not identify the people who used the road or establish that a hidden settlement lies beyond it.

events.title: THE CONFIDENTIAL DISPATCH TO CELER REMAINS WITHOUT A REPLY
events.body: The expedition's correspondence register records that the confidential dispatch sent toward Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer has not yet produced a reply. Valerius does not treat the silence as confirmation of any theory about the engineered road, and the scribes keep the dispatch's observations separate from its hypotheses. The field party continues the investigation under its existing instructions rather than waiting for a political answer before recording what it can directly observe. The lack of a reply leaves the expedition's Roman political thread open and makes the preservation of the field record more important. No new Roman order or change of mission is received during the week.

events.title: THE FORMATION HOLDS TOGETHER THROUGH A NARROW SECTION OF THE ROUTE
events.body: The column encounters a narrower portion of the route where the ground restricts the intervals between the separate groups. Valerius does not abandon the loose-phalanx principle; instead, he shortens the spacing temporarily while preserving the distinction between the outer watch and the men inside the formation. Once the ground widens, the units open their intervals again and restore the earlier freedom of movement between sections. The exercise gives the men a practical understanding of when the doctrine can bend without losing its purpose. By the end of the day's movement, the outward-facing perimeter and the ability to reinforce another section remain established features of the expedition's field practice.

events.title: THE ESTATE STEWARDS KEEP THE WATERING ARRANGEMENT IN FORCE
events.body: The estate stewards continue the established watering arrangement with nearby smallholders while Valerius remains away. The access remains within the existing understanding and produces no new land transfer, payment, or alteration of the holdings. Workers continue the seasonal agricultural routine, while the stewards preserve the route record so that a practical local arrangement does not become an undocumented source of dispute. The household therefore continues its ordinary administration independently of the expedition's road investigation. No new financial realization is established by the week's local administration.

events.title: THE EXPEDITION CLOSES THE WEEK WITH THE ROUTE REGISTER EXPANDED AND THE COLUMN IN DEFENSIVE ORDER
events.body: The expedition closes the week at a temporary position from which the newly examined crossing and secondary approach can be revisited without losing the distinction between observation and conjecture. Valerius keeps the loose phalanxes in their established defensive arrangement, with the outer files facing outward and the interior open enough for movement and reinforcement. The route register now contains another damaged crossing, another uncertain line of markers, and additional observations about how the engineered corridor was laid out, but it still does not identify its builder or the people who may have used it. The private dispatch to Celer remains unanswered, leaving the political thread unresolved. The week's work therefore advances the investigation and strengthens the formation doctrine without forcing a conclusion that the evidence does not yet support.
